subject: McMurtry et al. (1992)
object: McMurtry et al. (1992) described a large kindred with familial benign hypercalcemia (FBH) in which 19 of 46 members studied across 5 generations (ages 1.5 to 91 years) were affected. In the 15 hypercalcemic subjects examined biochemically, serum immunoreactive PTH levels, measured in 3 separate immunoassays, rose to supranormal values by about age 30 years and appeared to increase further after that. Serum alkaline phosphatase and creatinine were normal, but inorganic phosphate was lower than in unaffected kindred members.

subject: McMurtry et al. (1992)
object: McMurtry et al. (1992) found that 3 of 5 affected adults older than 40 years who were studied radiographically had changes suggestive of osteomalacia. Iliac crest biopsy after tetracycline labeling in a 51-year-old affected woman confirmed defective skeletal mineralization. The authors suggested that the disorder may not be totally benign and that osteomalacia, perhaps due to mild hypophosphatemia, can develop in adulthood.

subject: McMurtry et al. (1992)
object: McMurtry et al. (1992) pointed out that in this kindred FBH in adults can be especially difficult to tell apart from primary hyperparathyroidism because serum PTH levels may be elevated. They suggested that the kindred might represent an unusual variant of FBH.

subject: Trump et al. (1995)
object: Trump et al. (1995) studied a 5-generation kindred from Oklahoma, USA, with 19 affected members, 2 obligate carriers, and 20 unaffected members. In this family, familial benign (hypocalciuric) hypercalcemia (FBH) occurred together with a developmental elevation in serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels.

subject: Trump et al. (1995)
object: In the Oklahoma kindred, Trump et al. (1995) tested 17 polymorphic markers from candidate regions: 3q21-q24 and 19p13.3 (FBH loci), 11q13 (MEN1), and 11p15 (PTH). Linkage to all of these regions was excluded (lod scores less than -2.00 at theta = 0.05 to 0.25). Analysis of multipoint crossovers and the LINKMAP program confirmed the exclusion.

subject: Trump et al. (1995)
object: Trump et al. (1995) named this form of FBH the Oklahoma variant, FBH(Ok). Because it was not linked to markers that segregate with FBH, MEN1, or PTH, the authors concluded that their results indicated further genetic heterogeneity and a third locus for FBH.

subject: Trump et al. (1995)
object: Trump et al. (1995) designated the FBH in the Oklahoma kindred as the Oklahoma variant, FBH(Ok).

subject: Lloyd et al. (1999)
object: In an Oklahoma family with a variant of familial benign hypercalcemia (FBHOk), Lloyd et al. (1999) carried out a genomewide search using microsatellite polymorphisms. They found linkage to 8 loci on chromosome 19q13, with the highest LOD score of 6.67 at a recombination fraction of 0.00 for D19S606. Recombinants placed the locus in an interval of less than 12 cM flanked by D19S908 and D19S866.

subject: Lloyd et al. (1999)
object: Lloyd et al. (1999) reported that linkage of the Oklahoma FBH variant family to the CaSR region on 3q and to the 19p13.3 FBH locus had been excluded. They suggested that a further CaSR or a mediator of calcium homeostasis is involved.

subject: Lloyd et al. (1999)
object: Lloyd et al. (1999) sequenced the calmodulin III gene, which lies within the 19q13 interval, in 1 individual affected with FBHOk. The sequencing covered the coding region, the 5-prime UTR, and part of the promoter, and found no abnormalities. The authors concluded that this gene is unlikely to be involved in FBHOk.

subject: Hannan et al. (2010)
object: Hannan et al. (2010) restudied the previously reported Oklahoma kindred with FBHH3 and investigated 40 members from 5 generations. They diagnosed FBHH from hypercalcemia together with a low calcium/creatinine clearance ratio (<0.01). Serum PTH was elevated in some affected individuals older than 30 years, and 3 affected adults older than 40 years had evidence of osteomalacia.

subject: Hannan et al. (2010)
object: Hannan et al. (2010) performed linkage analysis in 34 informative members of the Oklahoma kindred (19 affected) using 17 microsatellite markers and 7 SNPs. They confirmed linkage to chromosome 19q13, with a peak 2-point LOD score of 6.92 at theta = 0 for D19S606. Recombinants in 3 individuals refined the FBHH3 locus to a 4.1-Mb interval (<10 cM) flanked by D19S112 and rs245111. The interval contained 135 protein-coding genes and 24 predicted genes.

subject: Hannan et al. (2010)
object: Hannan et al. (2010) noted that the region of mouse chromosome 7 syntenic to the FBHH3 interval contains 4 Casr-related sequences (Gprc2a-rs genes), but BLAST analysis found no human or primate homologs. Comparison of the human (22.0 Mb) and mouse (39.3 Mb) syntenic regions showed 2 conserved segments that were inverted in man and an 11.6-Mb mouse region, containing 35 genes including the 4 Gprc2a-rs genes, that is absent from the human genome. The authors concluded that FBHH3 cannot be attributed to Gprc2a-rs abnormalities.

subject: Hannan et al. (2010)
object: Hannan et al. (2010) sequenced the coding regions and intron-exon boundaries of 12 candidate genes from the FBHH3 interval in an affected member of the Oklahoma kindred. The genes (including PTH2, PTGIR, GNG8, EMP3, SPHK2, TULP2, NUCB1, HRC, RCN3, CYTH2, RRAS and ATF5) were chosen for renal and/or parathyroid expression. No abnormalities were found, and RT-PCR excluded splicing defects, indicating that these genes were unlikely to cause FBHH3.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2010)
object: Nesbit et al. (2010) studied a kindred in which the proband was a 43-year-old woman. She had a corrected serum calcium of 2.74 mmol/l (normal, 2.15-2.55), a serum PTH of 47 pg/ml (normal, 10-65), and a urinary calcium clearance:creatinine clearance ratio of 0.006. She had no CASR mutation in the coding region or splice sites. Of 24 members from 3 generations of her kindred, 16 were hypercalcemic with normal or elevated serum PTH and mild hypophosphatemia, features the authors considered consistent with FHH3.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2010)
object: In this kindred, Nesbit et al. (2010) found that FHH cosegregated with microsatellite and SNP markers from chromosome 19q13.3, with a peak lod score of 5.98 at theta = 0.0 with D19S412. Analysis of recombinants placed the locus in a 3.46-Mb interval between SNP rs1990932 (centromeric) and D19S604 (telomeric).

subject: Nesbit et al. (2010)
object: Nesbit et al. (2010) noted that FHH is genetically heterogeneous, with 3 types: FHH1 on 3q21.1, FHH2 on 19p, and FHH3 on 19q13. FHH1 is caused by CASR mutations and accounts for more than 65% of patients. The authors suggested that FHH3 may explain the disorder in FHH patients without CASR mutations.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2013)
object: Nesbit et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing on 1 affected individual from each of 2 unrelated FHH3 kindreds, FHH3OK (Oklahoma) and FHH3NI (Northern Ireland). Within the 3.46-Mb FHH3 interval on 19q13.3, which contains about 110 genes, both patients had only 1 shared variant: a C-to-T transition in exon 2 of the AP2S1 gene, predicting an arg15-to-cys (R15C) substitution. The variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Restriction enzyme analysis showed that it cosegregated with the disorder in members from 4 generations of the 2 kindreds.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2013)
object: Nesbit et al. (2013) stated that the FHH3 locus lies on chromosome 19q13.3, in a 3.46-Mb interval containing about 110 genes. By comparison, the FHH1 locus is on 3q21.1 and the FHH2 locus is on 19p.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2013)
object: Nesbit et al. (2013) described FHH3 as a disorder of extracellular calcium homeostasis. Unlike FHH1 and FHH2, which usually have normal PTH levels, FHH3 is characterized by increased serum PTH concentrations, hypophosphatemia and osteomalacia. Patients with AP2S1 mutations were aged from 8 days to 78 years. They had elevated serum calcium and PTH and reduced urinary calcium excretion. In the FHHOK kindred, mean serum calcium was 2.88 mmol/l and mean phosphate was 0.77 mmol/l.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2013)
object: Nesbit et al. (2013) sequenced AP2S1 in 50 unrelated FHH patients (23 males and 27 females) in whom CASR mutations had been excluded. They found 11 heterozygous missense mutations, all affecting arg15: 4 R15C, 3 R15H and 4 R15L. The authors concluded that this was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance and that AP2S1 Arg15 mutations may cause FHH in more than 20% of patients without CASR mutations.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2013)
object: Nesbit et al. (2013) found the AP2S1 R15H mutation (CGC-to-CAC) in 3 unrelated FHH probands who were negative for CASR mutations. These were 2 females aged 19 and 49 years and 1 male aged 73 years at diagnosis, with serum calcium levels of 2.62 to 2.85 mmol/l.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2013)
object: Nesbit et al. (2013) found the AP2S1 R15L mutation (CGC-to-CTC) in 4 unrelated FHH probands or families who were negative for CASR mutations. In one of these, diagnosis was made at 0.02 years of age. Serum calcium levels ranged from 3.03 to 3.3 mmol/l.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2013)
object: Nesbit et al. (2013) found that patients with the R15C, R15H and R15L mutations had similar elevations in serum calcium and PTH and similar reductions in urinary calcium. This indicated no correlation between mutation and clinical phenotype.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2013)
object: Nesbit et al. (2013) found 3 different mutations affecting only arg15 in 13 unrelated probands, and noted that arg15 is significantly conserved in 5,400 human exomes (p less than 10(-10)). They concluded that this residue is likely a mutational hotspot.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2013)
object: Nesbit et al. (2013) noted that FHH1, FHH2 and FHH3 are genetically heterogeneous autosomal dominant disorders. About 65% of FHH patients have FHH1, caused by CASR loss-of-function mutations, and AP2S1 mutations accounted for more than 20% of the remaining cases.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2013)
object: Nesbit et al. (2013) noted that arg15 is conserved across AP2-sigma-2 orthologs and in human AP sigma paralogs. Crystal structure analysis showed that arg15 forms key contacts with a glutamine at position -4 of the dileucine motifs of cargo proteins. The authors predicted that the R15C and R15L substitutions would reduce affinity for the dileucine motif. They noted that CaSR contains a C-terminal dileucine motif (RHQPLL, residues 1009-1014).

subject: Nesbit et al. (2013)
object: Nesbit et al. (2013) expressed mutant AP2S1 in HEK293 cells stably expressing CaSR. All 3 mutants (R15C, R15H, R15L) shifted the concentration-response curves to the right, with a higher EC50 for extracellular calcium than wild type (2.73-2.90 mM vs 2.53 mM). This indicated decreased sensitivity to extracellular calcium. The R15C mutant raised the EC50 above that of vector alone, which suggested a possible dominant-negative effect.

subject: Nesbit et al. (2013)
object: Nesbit et al. (2013) measured cell-surface CaSR by intact-cell ELISA. After stimulation with extracellular calcium, cells transfected with wild-type AP2S1 had a greater reduction in surface CaSR than cells transfected with the R15C mutant. This indicated reduced CaSR endocytosis with the mutant. Separately, replacing the CaSR dileucine motif (Leu-Leu1013-1014 to Ala-Ala) also raised the EC50, indicating that the motif is functionally significant.

subject: Fujisawa et al. (2013)
object: Fujisawa et al. (2013) reported a Japanese female infant with FHH3. Hypercalcemia was found on a routine laboratory test done for poor weight gain on breast feeding. At 49 days of age, her adjusted serum calcium was 13.1 mg/dL, intact PTH was 27 pg/mL, and her urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio was 1.29 mg/mg, indicating hypercalciuria rather than hypocalciuria. There was no evidence of hyperparathyroidism, a PTHrP-producing neoplasm, or vitamin D excess.

subject: Fujisawa et al. (2013)
object: In a Japanese infant with hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria, Fujisawa et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous p.Arg15Leu mutation in the AP2S1 gene. The authors described the mutation as presumably de novo; it had previously been reported as a cause of FHH3. No pathologic mutation was found in CASR or GNA11.

subject: Fujisawa et al. (2013)
object: Fujisawa et al. (2013) concluded that the absence of hypocalciuria does not necessarily argue against an AP2S1 mutation. They suggested that the patient's early infantile age played a role in her hypercalciuria.

subject: Fujisawa et al. (2013)
object: Fujisawa et al. (2013) treated the infant with a low-calcium formula containing 2.6 mg/dL of calcium. She showed catch-up growth, and both her serum calcium and her urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio fell. Feeding a 2:1 mixture of low-calcium and standard formula then kept her serum calcium at about 12 mg/dL without markedly raising serum PTH. The authors concluded that low-calcium formula is worth trying in infants with FHH.

subject: Howles et al. (2016)
object: Howles et al. (2016) described 3 unrelated probands with familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia type 3 (FHH3) and heterozygous AP2S1 mutations: a 34-year-old woman with a 12-year history of hypercalcemia who had fatigue, headaches, and persistent generalized aches that did not resolve after parathyroidectomy; a 22-year-old man with hypercalcemia, fatigue, and generalized rib pain; and a 52-year-old woman with an approximately 20-year history of hypercalcemia who had headaches, abdominal pain, vomiting, fatigue, and musculoskeletal pain that did not resolve after pamidronate infusion or parathyroidectomy.

subject: Howles et al. (2016)
object: Howles et al. (2016) identified a heterozygous AP2S1 mutation causing an Arg15Cys (R15C) substitution in 1 of 3 unrelated probands with FHH3.

subject: Howles et al. (2016)
object: Howles et al. (2016) identified a heterozygous AP2S1 mutation causing an Arg15His (R15H) substitution in 1 of 3 unrelated probands with FHH3.

subject: Howles et al. (2016)
object: Howles et al. (2016) identified a heterozygous AP2S1 mutation causing an Arg15Leu (R15L) substitution in 1 of 3 unrelated probands with FHH3.

subject: Howles et al. (2016)
object: Howles et al. (2016) found that cinacalcet (10 nM) corrected the abnormal intracellular calcium signaling and MAPK responses to extracellular calcium in cells expressing the calcium-sensing receptor and the Cys15, His15, or Leu15 AP2-sigma mutants, indicating that allosteric modulation of CASR can correct the loss of function caused by AP2S1 mutations.

subject: Howles et al. (2016)
object: Howles et al. (2016) treated 3 FHH3 probands with oral cinacalcet (30 to 60 mg daily) over 33 to 45 months, resulting in more than 20% reductions in serum calcium and abatement of symptoms; serum phosphate increased and PTH decreased, remaining within the normal range. No nausea, vomiting, or hypocalcemia developed, although the authors noted that long-term surveillance would be required.
